questions.prompt: What is an eigenvalue in the equation \(A\mathbf v=\lambda\mathbf v\)?
questions.answer: The eigenvalue is the scalar \(\lambda\) by which the matrix scales the non-zero vector \(\mathbf v\). The vector direction is preserved, although it may be reversed or stretched.

questions.prompt: Why must \(A\) be square when discussing eigenvalues?
questions.answer: The equation \(A\mathbf v=\lambda\mathbf v\) compares two vectors in the same space. Therefore the input and output dimensions must match, so \(A\) must be square.

questions.prompt: Find the eigenvalues of \(D=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&7\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer:
For a diagonal matrix, the coordinate axes are eigenvector directions. The scale factors are the diagonal entries, so the eigenvalues are
\[
\lambda=2\quad\text{and}\quad \lambda=7.
\]

questions.prompt: Write the characteristic equation for \(A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer:
Use \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\). Thus
\[
\det\begin{pmatrix}a-\lambda&b\\c&d-\lambda\end{pmatrix}=0,
\]
so
\[
(a-\lambda)(d-\lambda)-bc=0.
\]

questions.prompt: Find the eigenvalues of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\) using the characteristic equation.
questions.answer:
Compute
\[
\det(A-\lambda I)=\det\begin{pmatrix}3-\lambda&0\\0&-1-\lambda\end{pmatrix}=(3-\lambda)(-1-\lambda).
\]
Set this equal to zero. Therefore \(\lambda=3\) or \(\lambda=-1\).

questions.prompt: Find the eigenvalues of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&4\\0&5\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer:
This matrix is triangular, so the determinant is
\[
\det(A-\lambda I)=(1-\lambda)(5-\lambda).
\]
Set it to zero:
\[
(1-\lambda)(5-\lambda)=0.
\]
The eigenvalues are \(1\) and \(5\).

questions.prompt: Check whether \(4\) is an eigenvalue of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer:
Compute
\[
A-4I=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its determinant is
\[
0(-2)-0(1)=0.
\]
Since \(A-4I\) is singular, \(4\) is an eigenvalue.

questions.prompt: Check whether \(-1\) is an eigenvalue of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer:
Compute
\[
A-(-1)I=A+I=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&4\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The determinant is \(12\), not zero. Therefore \(A+I\) is not singular, so \(-1\) is not an eigenvalue.

questions.prompt: Find the eigenvalues of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer:
Compute
\[
\det(A-\lambda I)=\det\begin{pmatrix}2-\lambda&1\\1&2-\lambda\end{pmatrix}=(2-\lambda)^2-1.
\]
Set to zero:
\[
(2-\lambda)^2=1.
\]
So \(2-\lambda=\pm1\), giving \(\lambda=1\) and \(\lambda=3\).

questions.prompt: Find the eigenvalues of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-2&3\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer:
Compute
\[
\det(A-\lambda I)=\det\begin{pmatrix}-\lambda&1\\-2&3-\lambda\end{pmatrix}=(-\lambda)(3-\lambda)+2.
\]
Expand:
\[
\lambda^2-3\lambda+2=(\lambda-1)(\lambda-2).
\]
So the eigenvalues are \(1\) and \(2\).

questions.prompt: A matrix has characteristic polynomial \(p(\lambda)=(\lambda-2)^2(\lambda+5)\). List the eigenvalues and algebraic multiplicities.
questions.answer: The roots of the characteristic polynomial are the eigenvalues. The factor \((\lambda-2)^2\) gives eigenvalue \(2\) with algebraic multiplicity \(2\). The factor \(\lambda+5\) gives eigenvalue \(-5\) with algebraic multiplicity \(1\).

questions.prompt: Explain why \(\det A=0\) means \(0\) is an eigenvalue of square matrix \(A\).
questions.answer:
The eigenvalue condition is
\[
\det(A-\lambda I)=0.
\]
For \(\lambda=0\), this becomes
\[
\det(A-0I)=\det A=0.
\]
So if \(\det A=0\), then \(0\) satisfies the characteristic equation and is an eigenvalue.

questions.prompt: For which \(k\) does \(A=\begin{pmatrix}k&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\) have repeated eigenvalue \(2\)?
questions.answer: The eigenvalues of this diagonal matrix are its diagonal entries, \(k\) and \(2\). To have repeated eigenvalue \(2\), the first diagonal entry must also be \(2\). Therefore \(k=2\).

questions.prompt: For which \(a\) is \(3\) an eigenvalue of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}a&1\\0&4\end{pmatrix}\)?
questions.answer: Since the matrix is triangular, its eigenvalues are the diagonal entries \(a\) and \(4\). For \(3\) to be an eigenvalue, one diagonal entry must be \(3\). Thus \(a=3\).

questions.prompt: Find all \(t\) such that \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\t&1\end{pmatrix}\) has eigenvalue \(0\).
questions.answer:
Eigenvalue \(0\) occurs when \(\det A=0\). Compute
\[
\det A=1\cdot1-t^2=1-t^2.
\]
Set this to zero:
\[
1-t^2=0.
\]
Thus \(t=1\) or \(t=-1\).

questions.prompt: For which \(c\) does \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&c\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\) have only one distinct eigenvalue?
questions.answer:
This triangular matrix has eigenvalues given by its diagonal entries, \(2\) and \(2\). The off-diagonal entry \(c\) does not change the characteristic polynomial:
\[
(2-\lambda)^2=0.
\]
So for every value of \(c\), the only distinct eigenvalue is \(2\).

questions.prompt: A repeated eigenvalue is not always a problem for finding eigenvalues. Explain using \(A=\begin{pmatrix}5&1\\0&5\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer:
The eigenvalues come from the characteristic equation. Here
\[
\det(A-\lambda I)=(5-\lambda)^2.
\]
So \(\lambda=5\) is an eigenvalue with algebraic multiplicity \(2\). The repeated root is clear from the determinant; the extra care is needed later when finding enough eigenvectors, not when identifying the eigenvalue.

questions.prompt: A student solves \(\det A=0\) to find all eigenvalues. Diagnose the mistake.
questions.answer:
Solving \(\det A=0\) only checks whether \(0\) is an eigenvalue. The full eigenvalue condition is
\[
\det(A-\lambda I)=0.
\]
For example, \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\) has \(\det A=6\ne0\), but it still has eigenvalues \(2\) and \(3\). The determinant of \(A\) alone is not enough.

questions.prompt: Prove that eigenvalues of a diagonal matrix are its diagonal entries.
questions.answer:
Let \(D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)\). Then
\[
D-\lambda I=\operatorname{diag}(d_1-\lambda,\ldots,d_n-\lambda).
\]
The determinant of a diagonal matrix is the product of diagonal entries, so
\[
\det(D-\lambda I)=\prod_{i=1}^n(d_i-\lambda).
\]
This is zero exactly when \(\lambda=d_i\) for some \(i\).

questions.prompt: Explain why a real rotation by \(90^\circ\), \(R=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\), has no real eigenvalues.
questions.answer:
Compute
\[
\det(R-\lambda I)=\det\begin{pmatrix}-\lambda&-1\\1&-\lambda\end{pmatrix}=\lambda^2+1.
\]
The equation \(\lambda^2+1=0\) has no real solutions. Geometrically, a \(90^\circ\) rotation turns every non-zero real vector to a perpendicular direction, so no real non-zero vector stays on its original line.
